title: 1996 AHSME Problem 29
statement: If \(n\) is a positive integer such that \(2n\) has \(28\) positive divisors and \(3n\) has \(30\) positive divisors, then how many positive divisors does \(6n\) have?

solutions.text: Write \(n=2^a3^bq\) with \(\gcd(q,6)=1,\) and let \(t=\tau(q).\) Then \[ \begin{aligned} (a+2)(b+1)t&=28,\\ (a+1)(b+2)t&=30. \end{aligned} \] Hence \(t\) is \(1\) or \(2.\) Checking the factor pairs of \(14,15\) gives no solution when \(t=2.\) Checking those of \(28,30\) when \(t=1\) gives the unique solution \(a=5,b=3.\) Therefore \[ \begin{aligned} \tau(6n)&=(a+2)(b+2)t\\ &=7\cdot5=35, \end{aligned} \] so the correct answer is C.
hints: Write \(n=2^a3^bq\), where \(q\) is relatively prime to \(6\), and let \(t\) be the number of divisors of \(q\)
Use the two divisor-count equations to restrict \(t\) to a divisor of both \(28\) and \(30\)
